title: The Answer Was on Top
pace_basis: same runtime-anchored pace paragraph as 2026-09-19 and 09-23 (1.907 wps measured)
note: Numbers and acronyms written phonetically for the synth; on screen they render as numerals. Every factual line carries a claim id.

lines.text: A Kodiak woman asked Google when snipe season opens.
It said September first.
So on September fifth she shot three snipe.
lines.display: So on September 5th she shot three snipe.

lines.text: But the trooper's report says the general season didn't open until October eighth.
lines.display: But the trooper's report says the general season didn't open until October 8th.

lines.text: At home she checked one more place. Then she called troopers and turned herself in.
The trooper ran her exact search. He got the same wrong answer.
So it wasn't a one time slip.
She pleaded no contest and paid a hundred fifty dollars.
lines.display: She pleaded no contest and paid $150.

lines.text: She told the Beacon, I feel terrible.
Spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time A I has been cited. He expects more.
lines.display: Spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time AI has been cited. He expects more.

lines.text: Weren't there warnings? There were.
Google's help page says A I answers may include mistakes. Check more than one place.
lines.display: Google's help page says AI answers may include mistakes. Check more than one place.

lines.text: McDaniel says the one source of truth is Fish and Game's regulations and emergency orders.
So she paid. But look at that source.
Fish and Game's own page says its online regulations are simplified, and emergency orders can override them.
So it's a stack of summaries over one binding text.
Google didn't respond to a request for comment.
She dug past every summary to the regulations. That's the one move that worked.
The answer was on top. The date was at the bottom.
Fish and Game will mail you a copy.
Before you hunt, which page do you trust?
